canonical_plan.heading: ML-30 — Feedforward networks and single-hidden-layer universality
canonical_plan.old_exact_body: **Pages:** feedforward-networks-and-universal-approximation / feedforward-networks-and-universal-approximation-examples. **Scope:** Define a finite directed acyclic computation graph and layered MLP specialization, then define the single-hidden-layer realization x ↦ c+Σⱼaⱼσ(wⱼ·x+bⱼ). State Leshno et al.’s exact activation class: σ is locally essentially bounded and the closure of its discontinuity set has Lebesgue measure zero. The affine-ridge span is dense in C(ℝᵈ) with uniform convergence on every compact set iff σ is not an algebraic polynomial almost everywhere. Separately state the Lᵖ(μ) theorem for compactly supported finite μ≪dx and 1<p<∞, with the same iff condition. These are density/existence claims without a quantitative width bound; they imply neither trainability nor statistical generalization. Proposed items: def-feedforward-neural-network; def-single-hidden-layer-network; def-activation-class-locally-essentially-bounded-ae-continuous; thm-single-hidden-layer-universal-approximation. **Proof route:** polynomial activations produce bounded-degree polynomials and fail density. For smooth nonpolynomial activations use finite differences of translates to generate monomials and Weierstrass. For rough activations approximate convolutions by Riemann sums of translates; if all convolutions were polynomial, Baire category yields a common degree bound and a distributional derivative identity forcing σ polynomial a.e. Leshno cite, but do not prove, ridge-function density; discharge it locally by Stone–Weierstrass applied to the polynomial algebra on each compact set and polarization of homogeneous polynomials into powers of linear forms. Retain the convolution, common-degree, and distributional-derivative argument for the merely locally essentially bounded activation class. **Examples:** nonpolynomial ReLU/sigmoid; polynomial activation with bounded-degree obstruction; offset-free sine units remain odd and cannot approximate even functions. The topology is compact-uniform, not uniform on all ℝᵈ; offsets are essential in general. **Requires:** thm-real-stone-weierstrass-general for compact polynomial approximation; the polarization/ridge-density argument is local to this pair. No Category 3 dependency. **Sources:** Leshno, Lin, Pinkus, and Schocken, NYU Working Paper IS-92-13 (1992), complete source text read: Definitions 3–5, §4 Theorem 1, §5 offset example, and complete §6 proof Steps 1–7. This is the author working-paper text of the result later published in Neural Networks 6 (1993); Goodfellow, Deep Learning, §6.4.1 is an overview only, not the proof supplier.
canonical_plan.new_exact_body: **Pages:** feedforward-networks-and-universal-approximation / feedforward-networks-and-universal-approximation-examples. **Scope:** Define a finite directed acyclic computation graph and layered MLP specialization, then define the single-hidden-layer realization x ↦ c+Σⱼaⱼσ(wⱼ·x+bⱼ). For this broad class M, the affine-ridge span approximates continuous functions on every compact set in the Lebesgue essential-supremum seminorm iff σ is not an algebraic polynomial almost everywhere, as in the source’s Definition 5. Separately retain pointwise compact-uniform density for the subclass M_pt of actual representatives bounded at every point on every compact interval, with the same iff across all compact sets. The original broader pointwise-M reading is false, as proved by cex-pointwise-uniformity-fails-for-an-essentially-bounded-activation; retain its explicit H-plus-reciprocal-spikes witness. State the Lᵖ(μ) iff for nonzero compactly supported finite regular Borel μ≪dx and 1<p<∞. Use Borel representatives of raw networks equal Lebesgue-almost everywhere, preserving constant-input units exactly; prove existence and uniqueness of the resulting Lᵖ(μ) classes. State μ=0 separately: Lᵖ(0)={0} and every activation gives density, including polynomial activations, as cex-zero-measure-does-not-force-a-nonpolynomial-activation proves. Positivity of an arbitrary atomic measure does not replace absolute continuity. These are density/existence claims without a quantitative width bound; they imply neither trainability nor statistical generalization. Proposed items: def-feedforward-neural-network; def-single-hidden-layer-network; def-activation-class-locally-essentially-bounded-ae-continuous; thm-single-hidden-layer-universal-approximation. **Proof route:** polynomial activations produce bounded-degree polynomials and fail density. Leshno cite, but do not prove, ridge-function density; discharge it locally by Stone–Weierstrass applied to the polynomial algebra on each compact set and polarization of homogeneous polynomials into powers of linear forms. Retain the convolution, common-degree, and distributional-derivative argument for the merely locally essentially bounded activation class: first prove the Riemann-sum approximation for M_pt, then replace σ by zero on its closed null discontinuity set to transfer approximants for M in essential supremum and Lᵖ. For zero input weights absorb the exact constant values into the output bias; nonzero affine pullbacks of the exceptional null set are null. Prove the polynomial obstruction both on a segment in pointwise norm and on a full cube in essential supremum. The positive AC Lᵖ obstruction uses the proper closed finite-dimensional bounded-degree polynomial subspace. **Examples:** nonpolynomial ReLU/sigmoid; polynomial activation with bounded-degree obstruction; offset-free sine units remain odd and cannot approximate even functions. Distinguish pointwise compact-uniform and Lebesgue essential-supremum topologies; neither means uniform approximation on all ℝᵈ; offsets are essential in general. **Requires:** thm-real-stone-weierstrass-general for compact polynomial approximation; the polarization/ridge-density argument is local to this pair. No Category 3 dependency. **Sources:** Leshno, Lin, Pinkus, and Schocken, NYU Working Paper IS-92-13 (1992), complete source text read: Definitions 3–5, §4 Theorem 1, §5 offset example, and complete §6 proof Steps 1–7.
